name: English (Caribbean)
variety: Jamaican English, the standard English of Jamaica as spoken beside Jamaican Creole, taken here as the reference for the Caribbean because it is the best described and the closest to the eSpeak NG voice; other territories (Trinidad, Barbados, Guyana, the Bahamas) differ, above all in rhoticity
sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Volume 3: Beyond the British Isles. Cambridge University Press.
Devonish, Hubert and Harry, Otelemate G. (2004). Jamaican Creole and Jamaican English: phonology. In Schneider et al. (eds.), A Handbook of Varieties of English, volume 1. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Harry, Otelemate G. (2006). Jamaican Creole. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 36(1), 125-131.
Wassink, Alicia Beckford (2001). Theme and variation in Jamaican vowels. Language Variation and Change 13(2), 135-159.
Cassidy, Frederic G. and Le Page, Robert B. (1967). Dictionary of Jamaican English. Cambridge University Press.
Gooden, Shelome; Drayton, Kathy-Ann; Beckman, Mary (2009). Tone inventories and tune-text alignments: prosodic variation in 'hybrid' prosodic systems. Studies in Language 33(2), 396-436.
contrasts: FACE and GOAT are long monophthongs /eː/ and /oː/; towards the Creole end of the range they are falling diphthongs [ie] and [uo]
TRAP and BATH have the same quality [a] and differ in length (no TRAP-BATH split of quality); PALM and START also have [aː]
LOT is unrounded and may merge with TRAP towards the Creole end ([a] in both rat and rot); in the standard the two are kept apart
STRUT is a back rounded vowel, separate from FOOT
NEAR and SQUARE are merged for many speakers (beer = bear)
NORTH versus FORCE are kept apart ([aː] or [ɔː] against [oː])
vowel length is contrastive and not tied to large differences of quality

rhoticity is variable: Jamaican English keeps /r/ after a vowel mainly at the end of a stressed syllable (near, square, car) and less before a consonant; Barbados is fully rhotic, Trinidad and the Bahamas are non-rhotic, Guyana is variable
/θ ð/ versus /t d/ in the standard; in the Creole and in informal speech they fall together as stops (thin = tin, then = den)
allophony: /θ ð/ are often [t d] (TH-stopping), in all but careful speech
unstressed syllables keep full vowels much more than in British or American English: final -er and -a are [a] (letter [ˈlɛta], comma [ˈkɔma]), and prefixes keep their vowels

/k ɡ/ are palatal [c ɟ] or [kj ɡj] before /a/ in words that had a front vowel historically (cat [cat], garden [ˈɟaːdn̩]) but not in words such as cot, which keeps the contrast cat versus cot where the vowels merge
/h/ is variably dropped, and variably added before initial vowels, in Kingston and the east of Jamaica; the west keeps /h/ as a stable phoneme
final consonant clusters are reduced in informal speech (test as tes, hand as han)
/v/ may be [b] in a few Creole words
MOUTH is [ɔu], with a rounded back start
CHOICE may merge with PRICE in informal speech (boil = bile)
NURSE is [ɜː] with or without /r/ in the standard and a short back vowel in the Creole (bird as [bʌd])
/p t k/ are aspirated; /t/ is not tapped or glottalised
phonotactics: word-final clusters of two obstruents are often reduced to one
syllabic nasals and laterals occur (garden, bottle)
short vowels may end unstressed syllables with their full quality

stress.rule: As in other accents of English, with some words stressed later than in British English and with less difference between stressed and unstressed syllables.
stress.cues: pitch is the main cue; duration and vowel quality differ less between stressed and unstressed syllables than in British or American English

rhythm.vowel_reduction: weak: most unstressed syllables keep a full vowel; schwa is limited
rhythm.notes: Caribbean English is regularly described as syllable-timed or as nearer to syllable timing than British and American English (Wells 1982). I cannot quote a published nPVI value with confidence.

length.notes: Long and short vowels contrast, with small differences of quality (Wassink 2001 measured both spectral and temporal differences in Jamaican vowels). No long consonants.

intonation.declarative: rising accents on stressed syllables with a final fall; level or rising pitch at the end of a statement is also frequent, above all in Trinidad
intonation.continuation: rise or high level pitch at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: rising accent (L+H*) on the stressed syllable
intonation.notes: After Gooden, Drayton and Beckman (2009), who compare Jamaican and Trinidadian speech. Jamaican Creole is reported to have a few word pairs kept apart by pitch pattern alone (for example the kinship term and the religious title written mada), so pitch may have a small lexical role at the Creole end of the range.

tone.notes: No lexical tone in the standard. A small number of Creole word pairs differ by pitch pattern (see the intonation notes).

problems: the voice is fully non-rhotic (car [kɑə], farmer [fɑəma], near [niə]); Jamaican English keeps /r/ in words such as near, square and car, and Barbadian English is fully rhotic
NEAR and SQUARE are kept apart as [ie]-like and [eə]-like diphthongs; many Jamaican speakers merge them
the IPA trace labels FACE and GOAT as [eɪ] and [oʊ], although their formant data are monophthongs (vowel/e, vowel/o)
TH-stopping is applied to every /θ/ and /ð/ ('replace 00'), which fits informal speech and the Creole but not careful standard speech
there are no palatal stops before /a/ (cat, garden) and no reduction of final clusters

syllable timing is only approximated by equal length values for unstressed and secondary-stressed syllables (stressLength 175); primary-stressed syllables are still much longer, and the stress rules and reductions are those of British English apart from rule set 8
the tunes are the default English ones, and wh-questions get the rising question tune
good: FACE and GOAT are monophthongs in sound
final unstressed schwa is [a] (letter, comma, water), and rule set 8 keeps full vowels in some endings
TH-stopping with a dental stop for /θ/, and [ɪn] for unstressed -ing
LOT is unrounded, STRUT is a back rounded vowel, BATH and PALM are a long [aː]-like vowel
NORTH [ɔə] and FORCE [oə] are kept apart

notes: Speech in Jamaica ranges from the Creole to the standard, and speakers move along that range with the situation; the description follows the standard end and marks Creole features as such. In the consonant list [c ɟ] are the palatal stops before /a/. In the diphthong list [ie] and [uo] are the Creole forms of FACE and GOAT. I give no formant or voice onset time values: Wassink (2001) has formant and duration measurements, which I cannot quote with confidence.
